reason: The sources support a highly engaging story about 55 Cancri e's extreme 18-hour orbit, tidal locking, and massive volcanic activity, though the popular diamond theory is only in one source and must be noted as disputed.
story: Imagine a world where a whole year lasts less than 18 hours. Located just 40 light-years away, 55 Cancri e is a giant rocky "super-Earth" nearly eight times more massive than our own planet, orbiting so close to its sun-like star that it is trapped in a death spiral. Because it is tidally locked, one side permanently faces the stellar furnace, roasting at temperatures over 2,000 Kelvin—hot enough to melt iron. First detected in 2004, this extreme world has puzzled scientists for two decades. NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope made history by detecting its direct infrared light, revealing wild temperature swings likely caused by massive volcanic eruptions and towering plumes of dust. Most recently, the James Webb Space Telescope peered through the glare to detect a thick, volatile atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide, sustained by a bubbling magma ocean. It is a literal hellscape next door.
angle: A super-Earth just 40 light-years away has a year that lasts only 18 hours, featuring a permanent dayside so hot it melts iron and a thick atmosphere sustained by a giant magma ocean.

claims.claim: 55 Cancri e is classified as a "super-Earth," which is an exoplanet more massive than Earth but lighter than gas giants like Neptune.
The planet is approximately twice the size (radius or diameter) of Earth.
The planet has a mass of about eight times that of Earth.
The exoplanet is located relatively close to Earth, at about 40 to 41 light-years away.
The planet orbits a Sun-like host star named 55 Cancri (also known as 55 Cancri A).
The planetary system contains five known planets, with 55 Cancri e being the innermost planet.
The planet's orbit is so tight that it takes less than 18 hours to complete a full revolution, which constitutes its year.
The planet is tidally locked to its host star, meaning one hemisphere permanently faces the star (dayside) and the other faces away (nightside).
The dayside of the planet is extremely hot, with temperatures exceeding 2,000 Kelvin (approximately 3,100 degrees Fahrenheit).
The extreme temperatures on the star-facing side are hot enough to melt metal or iron.
NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope made history by directly detecting infrared light (thermal emission) from this super-Earth.
The planet exhibits dramatic temperature or transit variations, which scientists have attributed to large-scale volcanic eruptions.
Observations by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in 2024 confirmed the planet has a volatile atmosphere likely rich in carbon dioxide (CO2) or carbon monoxide (CO).
The planet's volatile atmosphere is believed to be outgassed from and sustained by a magma ocean on its surface.
The planet was initially discovered using radial velocity measurements (detecting Doppler shifts in the star's spectrum).

disputed: The diamond interior theory is only mentioned in [S1]. The script should treat this as a tentative hypothesis rather than a fact, noting that other studies in [S2] and [S3] suggested it was a water-heavy world, while recent findings in [S4] favor a rocky planet with a magma ocean.

Early studies [S1, S7] miscalculated the planet's orbital period as roughly 2.8 days, which Dawson and Fabrycky proved in 2010 to be an observational 'alias' of its true 18-hour orbit. The script should explain this as a case of corrected orbital data.

Early atmospheric analyses yielded highly contradictory results, with some reporting hydrogen/helium/hydrogen cyanide signatures [S1], and others finding no escaping hydrogen or helium. JWST observations in 2024 resolved this by ruling out a rock vapor atmosphere and confirming a volatile atmosphere of carbon oxides.
The exact distance to the system varies slightly in sources, being cited as 41 light-years in [S2, S5] and 40 light-years in [S3, S6]. The script should refer to it as 'around 40 light-years' away.
